sections.text:
Job, peace be upon him, is a generous prophet who has set an example of patience in the face of severe calamity throughout all ages.

Ayoub lived in the Levant, and was one of the richest people of his time. He owned vast lands, fruitful orchards, and countless farms for horses, camels, and sheep.

God blessed him with seventeen sons and daughters, and he lived happily and contentedly with his loyal and patient wife, who supported him in all matters of his life.

Job was a pious and righteous man. He thanked God for all these blessings. He was kind to the poor, sponsored orphans, and hosted passers-by.

But God Almighty wanted to test Job’s faith and patience, so that he would be a living example for every afflicted person until the Day of Resurrection.

The series of harsh trials began.

First, pests took over his farms, destroying his crops, then all his livestock died in a very short time, so he lost all his wealth and became destitute.

Job did not panic, but prostrated himself to God and said: “The Lord has given and the Lord has taken away. Blessed be the name of the Lord,” and continued his thanks to God.

Then came the greatest and most severe test.

The roof of the house collapsed on all of his sons and daughters, and they died in one moment!
He was afflicted with a serious injury that would shake mountains, but Job’s heart, full of faith, remained patient and hopeful and did not utter a single word of discontent.

The affliction did not stop there. Rather, Ayoub was afflicted with a very rare, incurable skin disease.

The illness was so severe that people turned away from him for fear of infection, and he was forced to live in an isolated tent outside the city.

Everyone abandoned him.

His relatives, friends, and neighbors, and no one remained with him during his ordeal except his loyal wife, who refused to abandon him.

His wife used to go out to work as a domestic maid to feed her sick husband, nurse him, and clean his wounds with all patience and tenderness.

The severe illness lasted for very long years (it was said that it was eighteen years), and Job was becoming more and more patient and satisfied with God’s will.

Even his wife, out of extreme fatigue and seeing his condition, said to him one day: “You are a prophet who has answered the call. Pray to God to heal you.”

He answered her with the modesty of the prophets: “I have lived in bliss and health for many years. Am I not ashamed before God to be frightened by a few years of illness?”

One day, the wife could not find work due to the extreme poverty of the villagers, and because she wanted to feed Ayoub, she was forced to cut her two braids (her beautiful hair) and sell them to buy a loaf of bread.

When Job saw this, he was deeply saddened by the state of his honorable wife, and only here did he turn his heart to God in sincere supplication.

He did not ask for direct healing out of politeness with God, but rather said with gentle words: “Indeed, harm has befallen me, and You are the Most Merciful of those who show mercy.”

The immediate divine response came! God commanded Job to strike the ground with his foot.

Job struck the weak, sick earth, and a spring of cold, fresh water burst forth!
God commanded him to drink from it to cleanse internal diseases, and to bathe with it to heal external diseases.

Ayoub did this, and in a few moments, all pain and illness disappeared from him, and his body returned to being young, strong and fresh, as if he had never been sick!
When his wife returned, she did not recognize him at first because he was so young, and when she realized that he was Job, she cried with joy and prostrated to God in thanks.

Not only did God heal him, but He rewarded him for his great patience by raining golden locusts on him to compensate for his lost wealth.

He gave him his family and the same as theirs, and provided him with good sons and daughters to compensate him for those he lost.

The eternal lesson from the story of Job, peace be upon him, is that patience in the face of affliction is the key to great relief, and that God does not forget His patient and thankful servants, and that affliction is not evidence of God’s wrath, but rather may be a sign of raising one’s ranks.
